text:
Anthropic Hits the Market, but Wall Street Hits the Brakes
JJ Kinahan is Senior Vice President, Head of Retail Expansion and Alternative Investment Products at Cboe Global Markets, Inc. (Cboe).
Wall Street came under significant pressure throughout most of Thursday’s session in what appeared to be a classic sell-the-news reaction. Anthropic’s highly anticipated initial public offering (IPO) sparked what looked like a rally in the broader market — until it didn’t.
Within minutes after Anthropic (ticker: ANT) began trading, the broader market rolled over. When the session ended, the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the S&P 500 Index and the Nasdaq Composite were all down more than 2%, finishing just a hair above their session lows. Technology and semiconductor stocks were the biggest culprits, but the selling reached nearly every corner of the market. Among sectors, consumer discretionary, communication services, healthcare and industrials all gave up 2% or better. Still, Anthropic closed 17% above its $83 per share opening price.
What happened? Let’s start with the story of the day: Anthropic. If the AI native company’s IPO was a test of investor appetite for artificial intelligence (AI), it crushed it. The record $81.3 billion raised and an opening trade at a 34% premium to its offering price appeared to demonstrate extraordinary demand. But investors hoping the blockbuster debut would rekindle passion for the AI trade story were likely disappointed by the aggressive selloff within minutes after the IPO hit.
As we’ve said before investors don’t appear to be losing interest in AI, but they do seem wary — and probably weary too — of many aspects of the technology, particularly the enormous costs. There may also be growing suspicion about many chipmakers’ relationships with China and the potential implications for U.S. export restrictions. AMD shares fell 7.7% after a short-seller alleged AMD’s ties to a China-based company could violate export restrictions, while a financial newsletter raised questions about circular financing, according to Barrons. The company denied both accounts.
There are other sources of anxiety too, including the prospect of higher interest rates and the ongoing tensions between the U.S. and Iran that might be adding to investor unease. The CME FedWatch tool is pricing in a 100% probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike of at least 25 basis points in December.
The Cboe Volatility Index ® (the VIX ® Index) is creeping toward 30, up nearly 15% on the day. We generally view that as a warning sign of potentially heightened fear in the market and volatility expectations. It’s not unusual for volatility to rise when a major IPO is launched or it appears market repositioning is in the works, but the VIX ® Index is something folks should keep an eye on.
It’s also worth noting that all three major indices have now dropped more than 3% so far in November, marking the first November since 2008 that all have fallen by that magnitude at this point in the month.
Friday’s session might be more telling of whether we’re seeing the final leg of an ugly November washout or whether investors step back in and buy the dip while staying within an unusually large range of volatility. Stay tuned.
